\chapter{Review --- Five Sets, Finished}
\label{ch:repaso-parejas}
\hlchaptermodality{256}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use every one of the sets the book had left half-taught.}

I can use every one of the sets the book had left half-taught.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(review)]{(review)}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-repaso-parejas}



\begin{quote}
Three places, in order. (\emph{Aquí}, \emph{ahí}, \emph{allí}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five chants, and each one finishes something.

\textbf{Places.} \emph{Aquí}, \emph{\textbf{ahí}}, \emph{\textbf{allí}} — one for each of \emph{este}, \emph{ese}, \emph{aquel}.

\textbf{Times.} \emph{\textbf{Ahora}}, \emph{\textbf{hoy}}, \emph{mañana} — now, today, tomorrow.

\textbf{Articles.} \emph{Un libro}, \emph{\textbf{unos}} \emph{libros} — one, then a few.

\textbf{Possessives.} \emph{Nuestra casa}, \emph{\textbf{vuestra}} \emph{casa} — and with that the set of six is closed.

\textbf{Two verbs.} \emph{\textbf{Vi}}, \emph{\textbf{di}} — the shortest pasts in the language.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a gap in a set is hard to see}]
Every one of these was a set you already partly had. You had \emph{aquí} without \emph{ahí}. You had \emph{mañana} without \emph{hoy}. You had \emph{un} without \emph{unos}, and \emph{nuestro} without \emph{vuestro}.

That is a particular kind of gap, and it is harder to notice than a missing subject, because nothing feels absent — you simply use the half you have and route around the rest.

And two small rules came out of it worth keeping. \emph{Vi} and \emph{di} take \textbf{no accent}, because a one-syllable word has nowhere else the beat could fall. And \emph{dar}, though an \emph{-ar} verb, takes the \emph{-er} endings in the past.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the five chants, in order
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many possessives are in the closed set? (\textbf{Six.})

And which place word matches \emph{ese}? (\emph{\textbf{Ahí}} — the listener's side.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — two pasts, both finished}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-repaso-dos-pasados}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}You all ate.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Comisteis}.) \textquotedblleft{}We used to eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Comíamos}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two whole tenses closed, and each closed on one small thing.

\textbf{The preterite} ran out of gaps when a single ending, \textbf{-isteis}, turned out to cover every verb that is not an \emph{-ar} verb — and the strong stems with it. \emph{Comisteis. Tuvisteis.} One syllable, and the last hole was filled.

\textbf{The imperfect} closed on \emph{comíamos}, and on the only three verbs that refuse the pattern: \emph{éramos}, \emph{íbamos}, \emph{veíamos}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Set the two imperfect sets side by side and one of them is covered in accents.

\begin{quote}
\emph{hablábamos} — one accent, in one form. \emph{comíamos} — an accent on \textbf{every} form of the set.
\end{quote}

That is not a spelling habit. In \emph{comíamos} the \emph{í} and the \emph{a} are two separate syllables, and Spanish would otherwise run them together into one. The accent is what keeps them apart — take it off and the word stops being a past tense.

And one verb sits across the line. \emph{\textbf{Dar}} is an \emph{-ar} verb, yet in the preterite it took the \emph{-er} endings and went as bare as \emph{vi}: \textbf{di}. I gave.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron} — then \emph{comimos, comisteis, comieron}
  \item \emph{hablábamos}, \emph{comíamos} — and hear where the stress lands
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending closed the preterite for everything that is not an \emph{-ar} verb? (\textbf{-isteis}, strong stems included.) And how many verbs break the imperfect? (\textbf{Three} — \emph{ser}, \emph{ir}, \emph{ver}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — the column that belongs to \emph{vosotros}}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-repaso-columna-vosotros}



\begin{quote}
The pronoun for \textquotedblleft{}you all,\textquotedblright{} in Spain. (\emph{Vosotros}.) \textquotedblleft{}You all go.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vais}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
These arrived one tense at a time, chapters apart. Collected, they are one column.

\textbf{Present.} \emph{Vais.} \textbf{Preterite, ordinary stem.} \emph{Comisteis.} \textbf{Preterite, strong stem.} \emph{Tuvisteis.} \textbf{And what belongs to you all.} \emph{Vuestro.}

Four forms, four different chapters, one addressee.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The pairing is what makes this cheap to hold.

\begin{quote}
\emph{nosotros} $\to$ \emph{nuestro}.  ·  \emph{vosotros} $\to$ \emph{vuestro}.
\end{quote}

Same shape, same ending, same job. Once you see the first pair the second costs nothing — and with \emph{vuestro} in place, the possessives have no gaps left.

Worth saying plainly: most Spanish speakers, across the Americas, do not use this column at all. They say \emph{ustedes} and reach for the \emph{they} forms. You are learning it because you will \textbf{read} and \textbf{hear} it constantly, not because you will be required to produce it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vais}, \emph{comisteis}, \emph{tuvisteis}, \emph{vuestro} — one addressee, four forms
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What belongs to \emph{vosotros}? (\emph{\textbf{Vuestro}}.) \textquotedblleft{}You all had\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Tuvisteis}}.) And who says these forms? (\textbf{Spain} — elsewhere \emph{ustedes} takes the work.)
\end{tcolorbox}
